What the original study did not say

Power poses

Standing like Superman for two minutes would change your hormones. Replications did not confirm it.

In 2010, Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported that holding an expansive posture for two minutes, hands on hips or feet on the desk, raised testosterone, lowered cortisol and made people take more risks. Cuddy's 2012 TED talk is one of the most watched ever.

What did not replicate

In 2015, a study with a sample five times larger found no hormonal changes and no change in risk-taking. In 2016, Dana Carney, the first author, published a statement saying she no longer believed the effect was real and explaining problems with the original analysis.

There does seem to be a small effect on how people feel: some report feeling slightly more confident after adopting these poses. The case became a symbol of psychology's replication crisis.

References

  1. Carney, D. R., Cuddy, A. J. y Yap, A. J. (2010). Power posing. Psychological Science, 21(10), 1363–1368.
  2. Ranehill, E. et al. (2015). Assessing the robustness of power posing. Psychological Science, 26(5), 653–656.
